To motivate the Uniform Center Theorem we first observe certain patterns in triangle types as illustrated in Figure 10 which shows the first seven rows of Tn,n−1 and Tn,n−2 for any sufficiently large n. The left hand panel, shows that in Tn,n−1 that for rows, 2≤r≤7 on diagonal d=1 and for 3≤r≥7, on d=2 the types are identical (triangles B and C in the figure). Similarly, the right hand panel presenting Tn,n−2 shows that for 3≤r≤7,d=1;4≤r≤7,d=2; and ​5≤r≤7,d=3 the types are identical (F, G, and I in the figure). These patterns generalize as follows: For n≥4​s,1≤d≤s, the triangles Tr,dn,n−s where s+d≤r≤n−2​s all have the same pre-type. By symmetry, the triangles Tr,r+1−sn,n−s also all have the same pre-type. These observations and patterns motivate the concept of the uniform center.
Definition 6.2.
Fix s≥1. If n≥4​s,1≤d≤s, the uniform center of Tn,n−s refers to the union of the following three sets of triangles:
Tr,dn,n−s,s+d≤r≤n−2​s,
(12)
Tr,r+1−dn,n−s,s+d≤r≤n−2​s,
(13)
Tn−s−d+1,pn,n−s,s+d≤p≤n−2​s.
(14)
The theorem statements will be complete and refer to all sides of the underlying n-grid. However, in the proofs we will only deal with (12) which lies in the upper left half. By our remarks earlier about symmetry, the proofs extend to the entire uniform center.
The Uniform Center Theorem simply captures the heuristic that the types of the triangles on each diagonal d,1≤d≤s are equal in a central region of Tn,n−s. Unexpectedly, the theorem can be proven without explicit computation using the methods of Section 4. Prior to stating the theorem, we present two easily proven lemmas which will be useful in the inductive proof of the theorem.
Lemma 6.3.
For s=1,n≥3,s+d≤r≤n−2​s, and 1≤d≤s+1 the pre-types of Tr,dn,n−s are identical.
Proof.
By Lemma 2.12 it suffices to prove the result for the upper left half. If d=1, then by Corollary 5.1, the pre-type of triangle Tr,1n,n−1,2≤r≤n−2,
is identically {23,1,1}. Also by Corollary 5.1, if d≥2 the pre-type of triangle Tr,2n,n−1
3≤r≤n−2, is identically {1,1,1}.
∎
Lemma 6.4.
For n≥4​s,s≥1,
The pre-types of ​Tr,dn,n−s,s+d≤r≤n−2​s,s≤d≤s+1, are identical .
Proof.
We first recall some facts about the s-grid. By Definition 2.13, the top and lower left corners of the subgrid Tn,n−s,s are located at r=2​s−1,d=s and r=n−2​s+1,d=s respectively. By Lemma 5.3 and considerations of symmetry, in the upper left half, (i) the pre-types of the corner triangles are {c⁡(s),c⁡(s),1}, (ii) the pre-types of non-corner triangles on the left side of the triangle boundary are {c⁡(s),1,1}, and (iii) the pre-types of triangles not on the s-grid boundary are {1,1,1} where c⁡(s) is as in Lemma 5.3.
It immediately follows that the pre-types (on the upper left half) of Tr,dn,n−s,d=s,2​s≤r≤n−2​s are identically {c⁡(s),1,1}. It also immediately follows that the pre-types (on the upper left half) of
Tr,dn,n−s,d=s+1,2​s+1≤r≤n−2​s are identically {1,1,1}.
∎
Theorem 6.5 (Uniform Centers).
For any s≥1, and for n≥4​s,
(a) 
In the uniform center each of the following three sets of triangles ⟨r,d⟩n,n−s,⟨r,(d+1)−d⟩n,n−s, and ⟨n−s−d+1,p⟩ have a single pre-type.
(b) 
The triangles satisfying (12), (13), or (14), are of the same type.
(c) 
For each defined s-subgrid Tn,n−s,s ( Definition 2.13) the interior edge labels are identically 1, and the boundary edge resistance labels are all equal.
(d) 
For triangles in the uniform center satisfying (12) the right and base resistance labels are identical, for triangles satisfying (13) the left and base resistance labels are identical, and for triangles satisfying (14) the left and right resistance labels are identical.
Proof.
Clearly part (b) follows from part (a). Parts (c) and (d) are simply a restatement of Lemma 5.3 and is included in the theorem for purposes of completeness. Hence, it suffices to prove part (a) and by remarks made above it suffices to prove assertions for the upper left half.
The proof uses an induction argument on s.
The base case, s=1 is provided by Lemma 6.3.
For an induction assumption we assume that for some s≥1, that
 for given d,s, the pre-types of Tr,dn,n−s are identical for s+d≤r≤n−2​s,1≤d≤s+1.
(15)
We proceed to prove this assertion with s replaced by s+1. There are two cases to consider according to whether d≤s or d∈{s+1,s+2}.
Case d∈{s+1,s+2}. This follows from Lemma 6.4 with s replaced by s+1.
Case 1≤d≤s. To prove the pre-types in (15) are identical, we must show that the right, boundary, left-boundary (if applicable), and non-boundary left (if applicable) edges are identically labeled. We do this using the lemmas presented in Section 4. We suffice with showing that all base edges are identically labeled on each diagonal, the proofs for the other edges being similar and hence omitted.
By the Base Edge Lemma and the notation introduced in Section 4, for given d,1≤d≤s and r,s+1+d≤r≤n−2​(s+1), we have
Tr,d,Bn,n−(s+1)=F⁡(Tr+1,dn,n−s,Tr+1,d+1n,n−s,Tr+2,d+1n,n−s).
(16)
By (15), the triangle arguments on the right-hand side of this last equation have edges whose values are independent of r. Hence the value of the left hand side is also independent of r as was to be shown.
To illustrate the subtleties of how the induction assumption justifies the transition from s to s+1, note that the upper bound for r in (15) is n−2​s, and that the maximum row value in the arguments on the right hand side of (16) is r+2. But n−2​s+2=n−2​(s+1), illustrating how the induction assumption justifies the transition from s to s+1.
∎
Corollary 6.6.
Conjecture 3.1(b) is true.
As indicated earlier, Conjecture 3.1 motivated the other results in this paper. Corollary 6.6 shows how the Uniform Centers Theorem which is used to prove this corollary could have been partially motivated by Conjecture 3.1. The next section provides a further example of how the Uniform Centers Theorem partially motivates the Main Conjecture.
